selected.headline: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
selected.evidence: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict Analysis: attack will force rethink of Trump strategy A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire and causing injuries, according to Saudi authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese were killed in the missile strike. The Houthis said a Saudi airstrike on Sana’a on Sunday hit a home and killed a child, as well as injuring six others. The Houthi government’s health ministry said coalition airstrikes over the last six weeks had killed 91 Yemenis and wounded 168, 60% of whom it said were women and children. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded in the Riyadh airport attack a day earlier. The Egyptian woman killed in the attack on the airport was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV. She was living in Mecca and had been returning from a visit to her sister in Riyadh when she was killed, the niece said. Saudi Arabia led an international coalition that intervened against the Houthis in Yemen in 2015 after the group took over Sana’a and toppled the Yemeni government. Recent Houthi attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure, as well as Houthi military advances, have pulled Saudi Arabia back into the Yemen war.

selected.headline: Ethiopia, Eritrea ramp up rhetoric: Are they inching towards war?
selected.evidence: Allegations of Eritrean troop incursions into Tigray deepen the rift with Ethiopia, as fighting in northern Ethiopia rages on. Ethiopia and Eritrea have exchanged accusations of aggression at the United Nations, raising fears of a new conflict in the Horn of Africa region as fighting intensifies in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region. The diplomatic spat comes as Ethiopian troops and allied armed groups advanced across Tigray, where forces from Asmara have allegedly crossed the border to support rebels fighting the government forces. The two neighbours, which fought a deadly border war between 1998 and 2000, were allies during Ethiopia’s devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war. However, they have since been at loggerheads over the 2022 peace agreement that ended a two-year civil war between the government in Addis Ababa and Tigray rebels, and over Ethiopia’s demands for access to the Red Sea. So, what did Eritrea and Ethiopia accuse each other of, and are they inching towards war? Eritrean troops had advanced as far as 60km (37 miles) into Tigray, Ethiopia told the UN Security Council on Friday, accusing its neighbour of violating its sovereignty. In a letter, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos described the alleged incursion as “a blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia’s inherent right to self-defence”. He invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises a country’s right to self-defence, but did not specify what measures Ethiopia was taking. He added that the latest developments suggest that the confrontation is no longer merely about Tigray. The war killed hundreds of thousands of people and was marked by allegations of massacres, sexual violence and widespread hunger. Rompel from Justus-Liebig-University Giessen said that the current situation is evolving. “The danger of a wider interstate conflict is real, and the situation has already moved beyond a purely diplomatic confrontation,” he said.

selected.headline: Russian strike kills at least 33 in eastern Ukraine in deadliest single attack this year - Egypt Independent
selected.evidence: Kyiv, Ukraine — At least 33 people were killed on Thursday when a Russian strike caused two public buses to catch fire in eastern Ukraine, local authorities said, making it the deadliest single attack this year. Another 18 people were injured in the attack in Kramatorsk, a city in the Donetsk region, which prompted authorities there to shut down the public transport system and urge people to move to safer parts of the country. “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” said Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.” The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) said the Russian strike caused a fire on two buses and in the surrounding area. Police in Donetsk said Russian drones targeted officers who were helping victims of the strike. Police were still working to identify the victims of the strike, with some bodies having to be pieced together from fragments, they said in a statement. Drones can be seen near the scene of the strike as responders load the injured onto stretchers and into emergency vehicles. One emergency worker can be heard asking an injured woman for her name. “Russia is bringing death to Ukrainian soil. It is striking our cities, killing our people, and multiplying its crimes every day,” added Filashkin as he offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of victims. A mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. Its southernmost anchor, Kostyantynivka, has now been effectively lost as a stronghold. CNN’s Ivana Kottasová and Jonny Hallam contributed to this report.

selected.evidence: ISLAMABAD, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Pakistan's president declared a state of emergency and suspended a provincial government led by the party of jailed former Prime MinisterImran Khan on Sunday, which the federal government said had failed to tackle Islamist militancy in the province bordering Afghanistan. The state of emergency and imposition of a new governor in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa sharply escalates a standoff between Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government, and comes a week after PTI supporters gathered in theprovince intending to march on Islamabad to demand Khan's release. The party’s last large-scale protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes with security forces and Khan’s 2023 arrest sparked nationwide riots that threatened the military’s standing. Hundreds of activists and three of Khan’s sisters have been detained ahead of the planned march, in what the PTI called one of the strongest crackdowns in years. Pakistan's constitution allows the government to take over from provincial authorities during an emergency, and Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said a provincial governor would take charge in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which has suffered an increasing number of militant attacks in recent months. Tarar told a news conference in Islamabad that the governor will initially be in place for six months, but could stay for as long as needed.The interior ministry said it would be deploying troops in the province. selected.headline: Major earthquake hits Panama, injures at least 27
selected.evidence: A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocked Panama on Friday, collapsing buildings and roads in the center of the country and injuring at least 27 people, with no deaths reported. The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System. The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia told AFP that there were no reports of fatalities so far. In Panama City, about 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers. "I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks. "Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking." A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall. Benjamin Gonzalez, 52, said he was at a farm near the town of La Miel when the quake hit, and when he returned home he found "many houses devastated" and "everyone terrified" in the small town square, which was left without power. selected.headline: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
selected.evidence: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". The US president's said President Volodymyr Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world". Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".

The government wants those projects to undergo one review instead of several reviews, and to have that single review completed within one year. The legislation is a core part of the Liberals' plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets. Here's what you need to know Ontario will begin removing bike lanes from a stretch on Bloor Street W. in Etobicoke on Tuesday, the Ministry of Transportation says. A notice of construction start, issued by the ministry, says the work will occur on a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road. Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, confirmed in an email on Thursday that bike lane removal will begin Oct. "Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday," Brasier said. T he Court of Appeal ruled in August that Premier Doug Ford’s government could rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said Thursday that the removal of the bike lanes is "completely unacceptable" and an affront to the city by Ontario Premier Doug Ford. "That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city. Whether it is bike lanes, speed cameras, Island airport, every element we need to have our say. The city belong to all of us Torontonians through the municipal government," she said. The ministry-issued notice says existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs will be removed and new pavement markings and signs "to safely restore" an additional vehicle lane in each direction will be installed. selected.headline: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus
selected.evidence: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. selected.evidence: In a matter of hours, an Iran-allied militia trounced Saudi-backed forces to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast. No one was able – or willing – to stop them. Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: In the weeks before the Iran-backed Houthi militia fanned out along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, sending their foes into a frenzied retreat, a Yemeni government commander called for help. It was obvious to the commander, Lieutenant General Tariq Saleh, that the Houthis wanted to seize his territory to reach the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the most important waterways in the world. Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates began a disastrous military campaign to restore the government. Hundreds of thousands of people died from violence, hunger and disease. Once again, Saleh found himself with a new sponsor: Saudi Arabia. When the US and Israel attacked Iran in February , the Houthis appeared willing at first to sit out the war. At least 500 of Saleh’s fighters were killed and more than 1500 wounded, according to a statement by his group. The Houthi death toll is unknown. In public statements, the Houthis sought to reassure the international community that they posed no threat to maritime security – only to Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s largest exporters of oil. Speaking by phone from their makeshift encampment, that soldier said that they had gone days without food.

selected.headline: FoN Campaign Defends Ghana's Expanded Fishing Zone
selected.evidence: Government has doubled Ghana's Inshore Exclusive Zone from six to 12 nautical miles for artisanal fishers — now Friends of the Nation is training coastal communities in Ahanta West to stop trawlers from crossing the new line. Barely days after a canoe fisherman in Butre spoke of his fears that marine protection rules could push small-scale operators further out to sea, an environmental NGO has launched a campaign aimed at making sure the opposite happens — that industrial trawlers, not artisanal canoes, are kept out of protected waters. Friends of the Nation (FoN) launched its "Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future" campaign at a day-long workshop held in Upper and Lower Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region on 11 October 2026, according to the Ghana News Agency (GNA). The workshop brought together fishers, fishmongers and other industry stakeholders to explain recent regulatory changes and the boundaries of Ghana's newly expanded Inshore Exclusive Zone (IEZ). The IEZ is a stretch of sea reserved exclusively for canoe fishers and other small-scale, artisanal operators, where larger industrial vessels are barred from casting nets. According to FoN, government has extended this protected zone from six nautical miles to 12 nautical miles offshore, effectively doubling the area set aside for Ghana's coastal fishing communities. Mevuta Donkris, FoN's Executive Director, thanked government for the extension but cautioned that the new boundary would only mean something if fishers themselves remained alert, GNA reports. A security researcher says data presented at a regional meeting in Senegal shows about 2,000 illegal migrants entered Ghana between March 2025 and July 2026, renewing calls for stronger border controls. 08, GNA – Friends of the Nation (FoN), a non-government organisation (NGO), has declared zero tolerance for mining activities in the ocean as part of its efforts to ensure justice in fisheries governance.

The declaration followed government’s proposed offshore gold reconnaissance deal, granting 10 contiguous offshore reconnaissance licences to Gold Coast Resources Ghana Limited to undertake gold mining in Ghana’s marine waters from Half-Assini in Jomoro to Winneba in the Effutu Municipality in the Western and Central Regions.
According to the NGO, gold mining in the high seas would disrupt the activities of artisanal fishers, thereby bringing fishing expeditions to a standstill.
Mr Mevuta Donkris, the Executive Director of the FoN, said this at a day’s workshop for stakeholders in the fishing industry at Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region.

It was organised by FoN under the project dubbed “Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future” and was attended by chief fishermen and women from Lower and Upper Dixcove, canoe owners, fish mongers, fishers, the Fisheries Commission, FoN and the media.

selected.headline: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender.
selected.evidence: Koch, at 103, has been perfecting his one-liners for decades. He deals them out quickly, with a half smile that reveals the four remaining teeth on his top gums and a flash of mischief in his clear blue eyes. After 63 years tending bar, he has his setup-pause-punch line down to a science. When a patron on a recent evening asks him whether he is the oldest bartender in the world, he doesn’t miss a beat. “Don’t ask me,” he says. “I haven’t been around the world yet.” By many unofficial accounts, Irv (as he is widely known) is indeed the world’s oldest bartender. The first of them, decades ago, was named Amy. “When the first one gets here, that’s when it opens up.” And after Irv’s wife and brother died, “he never stopped,” Cook says. Right now, he’s excited for his 104th birthday party in August. “But everybody should come on down and check us out while they still can.
